idiom_name: () / PhantomData<T> / Default::default(), no-op trait impl when a value is demanded
implementation_notes: Rust has no null, so a placeholder must be a value: () (the unit type) where a value of no interest is required, std::marker::PhantomData<T> where an unused type parameter must be carried, and Default::default() for concrete types that implement it, which also covers the zero-sized cases. When the parameter is a trait object or a generic bound whose methods the path never calls, the dummy is a struct with a hand-written impl whose bodies are no-ops - or unimplemented!()/todo!() as a deliberate fail-fast guard - and the callee side marks ignored arguments with a leading underscore or #[allow(unused_variables)]. The choice between () and a real struct matters beyond ergonomics: PhantomData<T> changes variance, drop-check and Send/Sync inference, so it is a placeholder that carries meaning for the compiler.
pitfalls: unimplemented!()/todo!() in a dummy implementation panics when the path changes - excellent as an unmissable guard, wrong as an unmarked placeholder; a no-op body hides the change instead, so pick that behaviour deliberately.

PhantomData is not a neutral filler: it changes variance, drop-check and auto-trait inference, so using it for a type parameter the struct never owns can accidentally make a type !Send or alter drop order.
A zero-sized dummy is free to construct, a struct with fields is not: adding configuration fields to a placeholder turns it into a hand-maintained stub nobody uses.
